findings.claim: Examiners regularly ask students to explain both.
findings.truth: No evidence supports a claim about how often examiners set this. The spec defines assessment objectives and formats only, not question frequency.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section (lines 106-125, 254-275); house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: the lateral blast killed 57 people, most of whom had refused to leave or were scientists and observers within the exclusion zone
findings.truth: 57 deaths is right, but the claim that most victims were inside the exclusion zone is not supported. The 18 May lateral blast devastated an area far larger than the official red zone, and the dead included loggers, campers, journalists and scientists at posts outside it. The unverified attribution is removed rather than reversed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens (57 direct deaths; red zone set 30 April, no support for the 'most inside the zone' claim)

findings.claim: These are the spec-listed ore minerals. Using an alternative mineral name that is not on the spec will cost marks.
findings.truth: The spec names only haematite and galena as ore minerals (with quartz and calcite as gangue), and names limestone, haematite and uranium for uses. Magnetite, chalcopyrite and sphalerite are not in the spec. The warning that a non-spec mineral name costs marks is invented.
findings.evidence: spec lines 444-446 (hydrothermal veins: gangue quartz, calcite; ore minerals haematite, galena) and 1309-1311 (limestone, haematite, uranium)

findings.claim: only spec-listed mineral names gain marks: haematite, magnetite, chalcopyrite, galena, sphalerite ... naming a mineral not on the spec, will cost you
findings.truth: Same error as F3, repeated as an exam rule. Three of the five named minerals are not in the spec, and no mark penalty of this kind exists.

findings.claim: Examiner reports repeatedly flag this confusion.
findings.truth: A fabricated appeal to examiner reports. The porosity/permeability point stands on its own.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: do not call it a reservoir rock in the water context, as examiners penalise cross-contamination of these terms
findings.truth: No such penalty is defined anywhere in the spec. The terminology advice is kept; the invented penalty is removed.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section; house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Chalk ... has moderate porosity in its primary pores and is highly permeable along its extensive fracture and joint networks
findings.truth: Chalk has HIGH porosity, typically 35-47 per cent. Its pore throats are tiny, so matrix permeability is low; that is precisely why nearly all flow is along fractures and joints. Calling the porosity 'moderate' loses the point the spec tests (analysing rock types for aquifer suitability).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Chalk: 'Chalk is highly porous, with typical values of porosity ranging from 35 to 47 per cent'; spec line 1315 (analyse rock types for suitability as an aquifer)

findings.claim: Examiners frequently set questions where students incorrectly apply oil-field terms to aquifer questions
findings.truth: An unverifiable claim about question frequency. The misconception warning is kept without it.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: If strata dip toward the reservoir, water can exploit bedding planes as pathways to seep under the dam ... Strata that dip into the valley sides (toward the dam structure) are generally favourable
findings.truth: The relationship is reversed. In engineering geology, beds dipping UPSTREAM (into the reservoir) are the favourable case: water entering a bedding plane travels down-dip away from the dam, so under-seepage is reduced. Beds dipping DOWNSTREAM are the hazard: they carry water from the reservoir under the dam to daylight beyond it, and the same planes act as potential slip surfaces. Separately, on the valley sides beds dipping into the hillside are more stable than beds dipping out towards the valley; the lesson conflated the two axes.
findings.evidence: standard engineering-geology dam-siting rule (beds dipping upstream are ideal); the lesson is also internally incoherent ('the rock is being pushed toward the dam') and contradicts its own St Francis Dam example

findings.claim: Competent (hard, unfractured) igneous or metamorphic rocks such as granite or schist make excellent dam foundations.
findings.truth: Schist is foliated and splits readily along that fabric, so it is anisotropic and a poor dam foundation. The same lesson two paragraphs later cites unstable schist as a cause of the St Francis Dam failure. Metaquartzite (a spec-named metamorphic rock) is the correct non-foliated example.
findings.evidence: spec lines 675-684 (named metamorphic rocks: slate, schist, marble, metaquartzite; foliated vs non-foliated textures); Wikipedia, St. Francis Dam (east abutment mica schist, severely laminated, on ancient landslide material)

findings.claim: [0].correct = 2 ('Into the valley sides, toward the dam structure')
findings.truth: The keyed answer marks the true answer wrong. Upstream dip into the reservoir is the seepage-minimising case. Key changed to option 0, and that option reworded so it carries the correct reason instead of 'so water flows toward the dam'.
findings.evidence: as F9

findings.claim: [5].marks: 'Strata dipping into the valley sides toward the dam' listed as favourable; 'Strata dipping toward reservoir: water exploits bedding planes to seep under or around the dam' listed as unfavourable
findings.truth: The model answer repeats the reversal of F9, so a student who wrote the correct geology would be marked down. Both bullets and the conclusion clause corrected to upstream = favourable, downstream = hazardous.
findings.evidence: as F9

findings.claim: [3].marks: 'A V pointing downstream ... indicates that the strata dip upstream' and 'the strata are dipping steeply enough in the upstream direction'
findings.truth: The rule of Vs is reversed in the mark scheme, and it contradicts the lesson's own Key Fact. A V pointing downstream means the strata dip DOWNSTREAM, more steeply than the valley floor; a gentler downstream dip (or horizontal beds) gives a V pointing upstream.
findings.evidence: rule of Vs as stated correctly in the same lesson's Key Fact (n4) and paragraph n3; spec Appendix B (constructing geological maps, dip and strike)

findings.claim: [0] 'V-shape pointing upstream' with options including both 'The strata are dipping upstream, against the valley gradient' (option 0) and 'The strata are horizontal or dipping gently downstream' (option 1, keyed correct)
findings.truth: Two options are true. An upstream-pointing V is produced by horizontal beds, by beds dipping gently downstream AND by beds dipping upstream, so a student choosing option 0 was marked wrong for a correct answer. Option 0 rewritten to a steep downstream dip, which genuinely gives a downstream V.
findings.evidence: rule of Vs; the lesson's own Key Fact (n4) states upstream-dipping beds V upstream

findings.claim: the Geological Society's Geological Code of Conduct (repeated in knowledge_checks[3].q)
findings.truth: The spec names 'The Geological Code of Conduct' in quotation marks with no publisher attached. The attribution to the Geological Society could not be verified, and the widely used UK fieldwork code is published by the Geologists' Association. The attribution is removed so the lesson matches the spec exactly; the keyed answer 'Geological' still fits.
findings.evidence: spec lines 354-356: "it is essential that all centres adhere to 'The Geological Code of Conduct'"

findings.claim: these are the three pillars the examiners look for
findings.truth: A fabricated claim about marking. The three-point advice is kept without it.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: For the 4-mark 'Sequence Geological Events' question type in the practical-skills component ... use a ruler - examiners mark construction accuracy
findings.truth: The spec defines no named question types and no fixed 4-mark tariff; it specifies only short, structured and extended writing answers. The examiner-marking claim is fabricated. Both replaced with neutral wording.
findings.evidence: spec lines 118-129 and 254-275 (assessment description)

findings.claim: The 2010 Haiti earthquake (magnitude 7.0) killed around 230,000 people
findings.truth: M7.0 is correct. The death toll is genuinely disputed: published estimates run from about 100,000 to 316,000, and 230,000 is close to the Haitian government's early figure. Defensible as written; not worth an edit.
findings.evidence: published range of estimates for the 2010 Haiti earthquake

findings.claim: a growing bulge on Mount St Helens' north flank - growing at nearly 1.5 metres per day
findings.truth: The bulge grew at 1.5 to 1.8 m (5 to 6 ft) per day. 'Nearly 1.5 metres' slightly understates it but is not mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens: 'this bulge grew by 5 to 6 ft (1.5 to 1.8 m) per day'

findings.claim: Before any major construction begins, a geotechnical site investigation is legally required in the UK.
findings.truth: Site investigation is required in practice by building regulations, Eurocode 7 and planning conditions rather than by a single blanket legal duty. Overstated but not mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: not in the spec; general UK practice

findings.claim: the dam had been built on a thrust fault zone, with weak Sespe conglomerate on one abutment that swelled when saturated and unstable schist on the other
findings.truth: The death toll (over 400; at least 431) and the two abutment lithologies are right. The San Francisquito Fault is normally described as inactive rather than as an active thrust zone, and the modern accepted trigger is ancient landslide material in the mica schist of the east abutment rather than the fault itself. Close enough for GCSE; left as written.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, St. Francis Dam (at least 431 deaths; west abutment reddish conglomerate and sandstone that lost rock strength when wet; east abutment laminated mica schist on ancient landslide; inactive San Francisquito Fault)

findings.claim: Every 6-mark question in all seven lessons is typed '6 marks - Extended Response (QER)', and every band ladder uses 'Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging'.
findings.truth: The Geology spec never uses 'QER'; it asks only for short, structured and extended writing answers, and it sets no 6-mark tariff. The QER label is a WJEC Geography convention borrowed into a Geology unit, and the four band names are not the house vocabulary (Top band / Upper-mid band / Mid band / Lower-mid band / Low band). Neither is a banned string, and both are unit-wide (probably corpus-wide), so this is a labelling ruling rather than a fact fix. Recommendation: leave in this unit and settle it as a corpus-wide relabel, since fixing it here alone would make Geology inconsistent with every other subject.
findings.evidence: spec lines 106-129, 254-275; grep for 'QER' in the spec returns nothing

findings.claim: What geological event caused the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill?
findings.truth: A well blowout is an engineering failure, not a geological event. The answer text is accurate; only the question's framing is loose. Not mark-affecting.
findings.evidence: internal consistency

findings.claim: Bring map reading, field observation, graphic logs and geological histories together to investigate a real area.
findings.truth: 111 characters, over the 100-character validator limit for lesson descriptions. Pre-existing, not a fact error; flagged for whoever next touches this row.
findings.evidence: validator limit in CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md

summary: Seven lessons checked. Two reversed relationships drive the HIGH findings: the dip-of-strata rule for dam siting in L6 (upstream/downstream inverted in the prose, the knowledge check key and the extended-response model answer) and the rule of Vs in L7 (the practice mark scheme inverted, contradicting the lesson's own correct Key Fact, plus a knowledge check with two true options). The rest are a cluster of fabricated examiner claims across five lessons, an invented 'spec-listed ore minerals' mark rule in L3 that contradicts the spec, chalk porosity called moderate when it is 35-47 per cent, and schist named as an excellent dam foundation. Assessment claims otherwise match the spec: no board named, no tiers, no SPaG, no 'Component' codes, and the map-based practical component is described correctly.
